column4: ## Old Covenant Washings - Historical Context
column5: ## Old Testament Washings - Historical Background

column4: In the Old Covenant, ceremonial washings played a central role in maintaining ritual purity and symbolizing holiness before God. These washings were prescribed in the Law of Moses and applied both to the priests who served in the Tabernacle and to the people of Israel. For example, priests were required to wash their hands and feet at the bronze basin before entering the Tabernacle or approaching the altar, symbolizing their readiness to serve in the presence of a holy God (Exodus 30:18-21). Similarly, rituals for cleansing individuals from defilement, such as contact with a dead body or skin diseases, involved washing with water as a sign of restoration to purity (Leviticus 14:8; Numbers 19:17-19). These acts served as outward demonstrations of an inward desire for holiness, emphasizing the importance of being set apart for God.
column5: In the Old Testament, ceremonial washings occupied a central place in maintaining ritual purity and symbolizing holiness before God. These washings were prescribed in the Mosaic Law and applied both to the priests who served in the Tabernacle and to the people of Israel. For example, before entering the Tabernacle or approaching the altar, the priests had to wash their hands and feet at the bronze basin, symbolizing their readiness to serve before a holy God (Exodus 30:18-21). Likewise, the ceremonies for cleansing those who were unclean due to impurity—such as touching a corpse or having a skin disease—included washing with water as a sign of the restoration of purity (Leviticus 14:8; Numbers 19:17-19). These practices were outward expressions of an inward longing for holiness, emphasizing the importance of being set apart for God.

column4: The ceremonial washings in the Old Testament required regular repetition to maintain ritual purity. Unlike permanent solutions, these rituals only provided temporary external cleansing, leaving the deeper issue of sin unresolved. The writer of Hebrews highlights this limitation, explaining that these practices were “symbolic for the present time,” unable to clear the conscience of the worshiper (Hebrews 9:9-10). These washings acted as constant reminders of human imperfection and the need for something greater-an ultimate purification that could cleanse not just the body, but the heart and soul as well.
column5: The ceremonial washings in the Old Testament had to be repeated regularly to maintain ritual purity. Unlike a permanent solution, these rites provided only temporary outward cleansing and could not address the deeper problem of sin. The author of Hebrews underscores this limitation, explaining that these practices were “symbolic for the present time,” and could not cleanse the conscience of the worshiper (Hebrews 9:9-10). These washings served as continual reminders of human insufficiency and the need for something greater—a final cleansing that could purify not only the body but also the heart and soul.

column4: The ceremonial washings of the Old Covenant find their fulfillment in Christ, who provides complete and eternal cleansing through His sacrifice. Unlike the temporary rituals of the law, Christ’s blood purifies fully, cleansing not just the flesh but also the conscience (Hebrews 9:13-14). Through His death and resurrection, Jesus accomplished what the Old Testament rituals could only foreshadow-true reconciliation with God. Hebrews 10:22 calls believers to “draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.” This language ties Christ’s work to the imagery of Old Testament washings while showing its far superior efficacy. His sacrifice does not merely cover sin but removes it completely (1 John 1:7). In this way, the ceremonial washings served as a shadow, pointing to the deeper cleansing that only Christ could provide, fulfilling humanity’s need for holiness through divine intervention.
column5: The ceremonial washings of the Old Testament are fulfilled in Christ, who through His own sacrifice provides complete and eternal cleansing. Unlike the temporary rites of the Law, the blood of Christ brings perfect cleansing, purifying not only the flesh but also the conscience (Hebrews 9:13-14). Through His death and resurrection, Jesus accomplished what the Old Testament rites could only foreshadow—true reconciliation with God. Hebrews 10:22 calls believers to “draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.” These words link Christ’s work with the imagery of Old Testament washings while demonstrating its far superior effect. His sacrifice does not merely cover sin but completely removes it (1 John 1:7). Thus, the ceremonial washings of the Old Testament were like shadows, pointing to the deeper cleansing only Christ can provide, fulfilling humanity’s need for holiness through God’s intervention.

column4: To reiterate this point, Christians are under no obligation to perform any ceremonial washing. Washings did not provide salvation under the old covenant and do not provide salvation in the new covenant. Ceremonial washing will not increase our standing with God, nor gain us favor. Paul strongly condemns the Judaizers of Galatia (read Galatians) who tried to mix in requirements of the Jewish context as necessary for salvation (e.g., circumcision). Salvation is by faith in Jesus alone!

column4: ## John’s Baptism
column5: ## John’s Baptism

column4: In the New Testament canon there are several baptisms mentioned. We’ve already discussed the baptisms and washings of the Jewish tradition.

column4: John the Baptist’s ministry centered on preparing the way for the coming of Jesus Christ. His baptism, described as a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins (Mark 1:4), called people to confess their sins, turn their hearts back to God, and prepare for the arrival of the Messiah. It served as an outward sign of inward repentance, symbolizing a desire for spiritual cleansing and readiness for the kingdom of God. John’s baptism, however, was temporary and preparatory-it pointed forward to the greater work that Christ would accomplish. While John’s baptism focused on repentance, it did not provide complete forgiveness or spiritual regeneration, as it lacked the indwelling and empowerment of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 3:11-12). Instead, John openly declared that one greater than He was coming, who would baptize not only with water but with the Holy Spirit and fire (Luke 3:16).
column5: John the Baptist’s ministry centered on preparing the way for the coming of Jesus Christ. His baptism, described as “a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins” (Mark 1:4), called people to confess their sins, turn their hearts to God, and prepare themselves for the coming of the Messiah. It was an outward sign of an inward heart of repentance, symbolizing a longing for spiritual cleansing and readiness for the kingdom of God. However, John’s baptism was temporary and preparatory - it pointed to the greater work that Christ would accomplish. Though it emphasized repentance, John’s baptism did not provide complete forgiveness or spiritual rebirth, because it lacked the indwelling and empowering of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 3:11-12). Instead, John publicly declared that One greater than he would come, who would baptize not only with water but with the Holy Spirit and fire (Luke 3:16).

column4: John’s baptism was fulfilled and surpassed through the death, burial, and resurrection of Jesus Christ. Christian baptism, instituted by Jesus and practiced by the apostles, signifies a deeper reality-union with Christ, death to sin, and resurrection to new life (Romans 6:3-4). Unlike John’s baptism, Christian baptism is directly connected to faith in Jesus’ atoning sacrifice and the indwelling of the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:38). The arrival of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost marked the new covenant and the beginning of Spirit-empowered living, which John’s baptism could not provide. Because of this, John’s baptism is no longer practiced, as it has been replaced by the baptism commanded by Christ (Matthew 28:19), which incorporates repentance, faith, and the sealing of believers by the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13-14).

Therefore, John’s baptism is no longer practiced, because it has been replaced by the baptism ordained by Christ (Matthew 28:19); this baptism includes repentance, faith, and the sealing of believers with the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13-14).

column4: ## Christ’s Baptism
column5: ## Christ’s Baptism

column4: Christ’s baptism set a powerful example for His followers and established the foundation for the Christian practice of water baptism. Though Jesus was without sin, He submitted to baptism by John to “fulfill all righteousness” (Matthew 3:15). In doing so, He identified with humanity’s need for repentance and pointed forward to His own death, burial, and resurrection. At His baptism, the Holy Spirit descended like a dove, and the Father declared, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:16-17). This moment marked the beginning of Jesus’ public ministry and revealed the unity of the Father, Son, and Spirit, foreshadowing the spiritual transformation believers would experience through faith in Christ.
column5: Christ’s baptism set a powerful example for His followers and laid the foundation for Christian water baptism. Although Jesus had no sin, He nevertheless submitted to John’s baptism in order to “fulfill all righteousness” (Matthew 3:15). In this way, He identified with humanity’s need for repentance and pointed to His own death, burial, and resurrection. At His baptism, the Holy Spirit descended like a dove, and the Father declared, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:16-17). This moment marked the beginning of Jesus’ public ministry and revealed the unity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, foreshadowing the spiritual transformation believers would experience through faith in Christ.

column4: Jesus later commanded His followers to be baptized, commissioning them to “go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). Water baptism, as instituted by Christ, became an **act of obedience** and a **public declaration of faith** for believers. It represents their identification with Jesus’ death, burial, and resurrection (Romans 6:3-4). Going under the water symbolizes dying to sin, and coming up out of the water illustrates rising to new life in Christ (Colossians 2:12). Yet, it is crucial to clarify that this outward act is not the source of salvation but a **visible sign** of the **inner work of grace** already accomplished by the blood of Jesus.
column5: Later, Jesus gave His disciples the command concerning baptism, sending them, “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). The water baptism instituted by Christ became an **act of obedience** and a **public confession of faith** for believers. It represents the believer’s identification with Jesus’ death, burial, and resurrection (Romans 6:3-4). Going down into the water symbolizes dying to sin, and coming up out of the water signifies being raised to new life in Christ (Colossians 2:12). However, it must be made clear that this outward act is not the source of salvation, but is a **visible sign** marking the **inward work of grace** already accomplished by the blood of Jesus.

column4: Water baptism is a **symbol** of the cleansing power of Christ’s blood and the renewal of the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 5:26; Titus 3:5). It signifies repentance, faith, and a commitment to follow Jesus. It is an outward testimony of an inward transformation-a way for believers to publicly declare their allegiance to Christ and their participation in the body of Christ, the Church (Acts 2:41). While it is commanded by Jesus and modeled in the early Church, it does not **save** a person. Salvation is by grace through faith alone (Ephesians 2:8-9), and the true cleansing occurs spiritually through the blood of Christ (Revelation 1:5). Water baptism is a response to that salvation, an act of obedience rather than a requirement for it.
column5: Water baptism is a symbol of the cleansing power of Christ’s precious blood and the renewal of the Holy Spirit（Ephesians 5:26；Titus 3:5）. It indicates repentance, faith, and a commitment to follow Jesus. It is an outward witness of an inward transformation - a way for believers to publicly declare their loyalty to Christ and their participation in the body of Christ (the church)（Acts 2:41）. Although it is commanded by Jesus and exemplified in the early church, it does not save. Salvation is by grace alone, through faith（Ephesians 2:8-9）, and true cleansing is accomplished on a spiritual level through the blood of Christ（Revelation 1:5）. Water baptism is a response to that salvation, an act of obedience, not a requirement for being saved.

column4: In the New Testament, water baptism is consistently tied to **repentance and faith** (Acts 2:38; Mark 16:16), both of which require a personal decision to follow Christ-something infants are not capable of making. Baptism symbolizes a believer’s deliberate identification with Christ’s death, burial, and resurrection (Romans 6:3-4), as well as their commitment to live in obedience to Him. Some denominations (e.g., Catholics, Lutherans) practice infant baptism as a covenantal sign akin to circumcision, however because infants cannot express personal faith or repentance, the practice of **infant baptism** does not align with the biblical model of **believer’s baptism**. Instead, many churches practice **dedication ceremonies** for infants, following the example of Hannah dedicating Samuel to the Lord (1 Samuel 1:27-28) and Mary and Joseph presenting Jesus at the temple (Luke 2:22). Dedication is not a substitute for baptism but rather a commitment by parents to raise their child in the faith, teaching them God’s Word, and modeling a godly life until the child is old enough to make their own decision to follow Christ and be baptized.
column5: In the New Testament, water baptism is consistently associated with repentance and faith（Acts 2:38；Mark 16:16）, and both require a personal decision to follow Christ - something infants cannot make. Baptism symbolizes the believer’s intentional identification with Christ’s death, burial, and resurrection（Romans 6:3-4）, and their resolve to live in obedience to Him. Some denominations (e.g., Roman Catholic, Lutheran) practice infant baptism as a covenant sign similar to circumcision; however, since infants cannot express personal faith or repentance, the practice of infant baptism is not consistent with the biblical model of believer’s baptism. Instead, many churches hold baby dedication services, following Hannah’s example of dedicating Samuel to the Lord（1 Samuel 1:27-28）and Mary and Joseph presenting Jesus in the temple（Luke 2:22）. A dedication is not a substitute for baptism, but a commitment by parents to raise their children in the faith, teach them God’s word, and model a godly life until the child is mature enough to decide to follow Christ and be baptized.

column4: Unlike the **ceremonial washings** of the Old Covenant, which required repeated rituals for purification, Christian baptism is a one-time event that reflects a completed work of grace. Old Testament washings symbolized external cleansing and foreshadowed the deeper spiritual cleansing that comes through Christ. In contrast, New Testament baptism symbolizes the inward renewal and rebirth accomplished by the Holy Spirit (Titus 3:5). It points to the believer’s participation in the new covenant, where cleansing from sin is permanent and based on Christ’s finished work.
column5: Unlike the Old Testament ceremonial washings, which required repeated rituals to attain cleansing, Christian baptism is a one-time act, reflecting the already accomplished work of grace. The washings in the Old Testament symbolized external cleansing and foreshadowed the deeper spiritual cleansing that would come through Christ. In contrast, New Testament baptism symbolizes the inner renewal and regeneration accomplished by the Holy Spirit（Titus 3:5）. It points to the believer’s participation in the New Covenant, where the cleansing of sin is permanent and based on Christ’s finished work.

column4: Water baptism is closely tied to the **promise of the Holy Spirit**. In Acts 2:38, Peter calls people to repent, be baptized, and receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. While water baptism publicly signifies the believer’s repentance and faith, the true baptism occurs inwardly when the Holy Spirit washes, regenerates, and seals the believer (1 Corinthians 12:13). This spiritual washing makes us members of Christ’s body and empowers us to live holy lives. The **Holy Spirit’s role** in baptism reminds us that salvation is not accomplished through rituals but through God’s transforming power.
column5: Water baptism is closely related to the promise of the Holy Spirit. InActs 2:38, Peter calls people to repent, be baptized, and receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. While water baptism publicly indicates a believer’s repentance and faith, the true baptism happens inwardly, when the Holy Spirit washes, regenerates, and seals the believer（1 Corinthians 12:13）. This spiritual cleansing makes us part of the body of Christ and empowers us to live holy lives. The Holy Spirit’s role in baptism reminds us that salvation is not accomplished through rituals, but by God’s power to transform hearts.

column4: It is important to distinguish between the **symbolic act of water baptism** and the spiritual reality of salvation through Christ’s blood. The Bible clearly teaches that salvation is based on faith in Jesus (Romans 10:9-10) and not on works, including baptism (Ephesians 2:8-9). However, water baptism is an **act of obedience** that publicly identifies the believer with Christ and the Church. It demonstrates an outward commitment to live as a disciple of Jesus, but it does not add to or complete the work of salvation.
column5: It is important to distinguish the symbolic act of water baptism from the spiritual reality of being saved through the blood of Christ. The Bible clearly teaches that salvation is founded on faith in Jesus（Romans 10:9-10）, not by works, including baptism（Ephesians 2:8-9）. However, water baptism is an act of obedience that identifies the believer with Christ and with the church before others. It indicates an outward commitment to live as a disciple of Jesus, but it does not add to or complete the work of salvation.

column4: Christ’s water baptism set an example for believers to follow, demonstrating humility, obedience, and preparation for ministry. For Christians today, water baptism serves as a public declaration of faith, symbolizing death to sin and resurrection to new life. While it is a command of Jesus and an important step of obedience, it is not required for salvation. True cleansing occurs through faith in the blood of Jesus, and the empowerment of Christian living comes through the Holy Spirit’s work in the believer. Baptism unites us with Christ and His Church, reminding us of the inward transformation and renewal that God has already accomplished.

column4: ## Holy Spirit Baptism
column5: ## Baptism of the Holy Spirit

column4: The baptism in the Holy Spirit is a profound and transformative experience promised by God to empower believers for ministry, service, and holy living. Every believer receives the Holy Spirit when they’re born again-this is how we’re made spiritually alive. But later, we should also receive the baptism in the Holy Spirit, which empowers us for boldness, spiritual gifts, and effective ministry.
column5: The baptism of the Holy Spirit is a profound and life-changing experience promised by God that empowers believers for ministry, service, and holy living. Every believer receives the Holy Spirit at regeneration - this is how we are made alive in the Spirit. But afterward, we should also receive the baptism of the Holy Spirit, so that we may receive boldness, spiritual gifts, and power for effective ministry.

column4: Water baptism is a public declaration of faith and symbolizes the cleansing of sin through Christ’s blood, Spirit baptism represents the empowering presence of God in the believer’s life. Together, these two modes of baptism form complementary aspects of the Christian walk-one as an outward sign of obedience and the other as an inward source of power and renewal. The baptism of the Holy Spirit is the Spirit upon us rather than within. At salvation all believers receive the Spirit within them, but when the Spirit of God comes upon them, they receive power and boldness for ministry.
column5: Water baptism is the public confession of faith and symbolizes cleansing from sin through the blood of Christ, while spiritual baptism represents God’s empowering presence in the believer’s life. As two forms of baptism, together they constitute two complementary dimensions in the Christian journey - one is the outward sign of obedience, and the other is the source of inner power and renewal. The baptism of the Holy Spirit is the Spirit coming upon us, not in us. At salvation, all believers receive the indwelling Holy Spirit, but when the Spirit of God comes upon them, they receive power and boldness for service.

column4: The baptism of the Holy Spirit is described in Scripture as a gift that is promised to believers and is received by faith. It is separate from salvation and is primarily for empowerment and witness (Acts 1:8). The baptism of the Holy Spirit is a gift of empowerment for believers, promised by Jesus and fulfilled at Pentecost. It is received through repentance, faith, and asking God. While laying on of hands is often used as a method, it is ultimately God who baptizes with the Spirit.
